etymology: Algonquian verb stem מִּיצוּ (miitsuw, 'to eat') with 1st person prefix נֶ־. The verb carries person marking inside itself—no separate pronoun needed. From Eastern Algonquian food vocabulary.
Lenape apuaan, the word for bread that emerged from indigenous bread-making traditions. Food vocabulary stays rooted in the land's practices.
Munsee/Lenape wigwaam, the word for dwelling that carries the whole concept of home. Can take locative suffix -ינְק or possessive prefixes.
Base וִיגְוָאם plus locative suffix -ינְק, marking place. Often combined with Hebrew preposition ב־ for emphasis: בְּוִיגְוָאמִינְק.
Algonquian verb with beautiful double meaning: the ringing of struck metal AND the ringing of voices in song. When things ring together—bells, voices—it's the same verb.
Algonquian adverb modifying verbs of sound or action. Softens whatever it accompanies.
Algonquian verb with built-in reciprocity—not just 'hear' but 'hear one another.' The relationship is inside the word's bones.
Algonquian perception verb. Takes נֶ־ for 'we see.' Perception verbs come from Algonquian because these languages encode sensory experience with such nuance.
Lenape təmakaan, the physical path walked. One of the anchor words connecting people to land. Takes locative -ינְק and plural -אַק.
Hebrew hayyom with definite article. Abstract time stays Hebrew; the physical path beneath feet stays Algonquian.
Hebrew na'ar. Abstract concepts of life stages come from Hebrew's prophetic vocabulary.
Hebrew tikvah, the great prophetic noun. Could not come from anywhere else—it carries centuries of yearning.
Algonquian verb suggesting fresh motion, something beginning to move. The physical stir that precedes abstract hope.

english: to walk well, walk in a good way
etymology: Magnificent polysynthetic Algonquian verb: not just 'walk' but 'walk well'—the manner fused into the verb. One word for what English needs four to say.
Hebrew compound: ב־ (in/with) + לֵב (heart) + טוֹב (good). Ethical vocabulary from Hebrew's wisdom tradition.
Algonquian verb showing inverse construction—an inanimate thing acts upon animate recipients. The relationship between actor and recipient can flip.
Hebrew dative pronoun. The little function words come from Hebrew.
Hebrew or, one of the great spiritual nouns. Physical fire might be Algonquian; spiritual light is Hebrew.
Algonquian verb for careful maintenance of things. Hand-work vocabulary from the land.
Hebrew kelim with masculine plural. Domestic vocabulary that would have been shared early in contact.
Algonquian verb for shaping and crafting. Physical making comes from Algonquian.
Algonquian verb for physical transport. Motion vocabulary from the land.
Hebrew pri. Agricultural vocabulary crossed over early.
Algonquian verb for radiance, glowing. Light-quality words from Algonquian.
Algonquian memory verb. When remembering the land, the language of the land carries the memory.
תְּמָקָאן with inanimate plural suffix -אַק. Paths as a category.

english: beside the waters, at the water-place
etymology: Fully Algonquian locative: the water-place with -ינְק suffix. No Hebrew preposition needed.
Algonquian verb for giving. With נֶ־: 'we give.'
Hebrew ezrah. Abstract ethical nouns from Hebrew.
Algonquian adverb expressing reciprocity, back-and-forth between people. Rich vocabulary for social bonds.
Algonquian verb for physical building and making. Concrete creation from the land's language.
Hebrew yachad. Communal action expressed as modifier rather than inside the verb.
The verb used as noun: the ringing, the song, the resonance of struck things or raised voices.
Algonquian number. Everyday counting from Algonquian; sacred numbers may use Hebrew.
Algonquian word for child. Kinship and life-stage vocabulary from the land.
Base אֲבִינוֹדְיִין plus diminutive suffix -שׁ. Endearment, smallness, young age.
Algonquian verb with 3rd person prefix וְ־. Bringing and carrying vocabulary.
Crucial Algonquian verb—fire-making was central to daily life and ceremony. With נֶ־: 'we kindle.'
Eastern Algonquian word for bear. Animal vocabulary from the land.
Bear with diminutive suffix -אֵשׁ. Endearing, small, young.
Algonquian verb with 3rd person marking. Domestic, restful vocabulary.
Hebrew noun נַעַל with Algonquian possessive prefix נְ־ ('our'). Hybrid morphology.
Triple hybrid: Hebrew noun + Algonquian possessive prefix + Algonquian locative suffix. Languages blending.
Hebrew gagim with masculine plural. Architectural vocabulary.
Algonquian verb with animate plural agreement -אַק. The roofs gather as living agents.
Hebrew ganim with masculine plural. Horticultural vocabulary.
Algonquian verb for rising/growing with animate plural agreement. Gardens rise as living things.
Hebrew atzot. Abstract governance vocabulary requiring formal register.
Hebrew participle. Councils deliberate in Hebrew.
Algonquian ishkotew (fire) with locative suffix. The fire that warms everyone. Base form for stove/hearth.
Algonquian voice/sound verb with 3rd person marking.
Hebrew chesed, untranslatable. Faithful love, covenant loyalty, lovingkindness.
Lenape lənuw (person) with animate plural -אַק. How the people are named.
Algonquian motion verb with plural agreement. The people go on.
Hebrew yadayim, dual form. Body vocabulary.
Hebrew kolot, plural. Sound as abstract concept.
Algonquian adverb for unity, gathering together. Rich social vocabulary.
Biblical Hebrew narrative opener. Kicks the wayyiqtol engine into gear—from here, every וַיִּ־ pushes the story forward.
Hebrew wayyiqtol passive. The narrative engine.
Hebrew wayyiqtol. Each verb advances time.
Algonquian minəkwaagan (cup) with animate plural -אַק. Cups are alive—they hold drink for people, participate in hospitality.
Hebrew phrase: stood + still. The frozen moment.
Modern loanword adapted to Hebrew orthography.
Hebrew-style compound: light + phone. Modern life, ancient grammar.
Discourse tracking particle marking the current center of narrative attention. No name needed.
Discourse tracking particle with obviative suffix -וָא. The other salient third person, 'offstage.'
Algonquian verb for seeking. Can enter wayyiqtol frame as וַיְּנָאטוֹנֵי.
Fully Algonquian compound: waasaakonenjigan, 'thing that makes light.' Ceremonial object.
Hebrew compound: cry-of-smoke. Modern device, ancient pattern.
Hebrew noun with feminine possessive suffix. The alarm's voice.
Hebrew noun used as infinitive complement: לְעֶזְרָה 'to help.'
Hebrew noun + Algonquian locative suffix. Hybrid morphology in action.
Hebrew hachoshekh with article. Abstract/spiritual vocabulary.
Loanword adapted to Hebrew. Light-bearing object.
Hebrew simile: כְּ (like) + אַזְהָרָה (warning). Comparative structure.
Algonquian verb in wayyiqtol frame! The singing/ringing verb describing struck spoons.
Hebrew wayyiqtol for bubbling, boiling action.
Munsee mbuy. Core element vocabulary from the land. Prenasalized consonant preserved.
Hebrew wayyiqtol for sliding. Comic repetition possible.
Hebrew phrase: sat + hard. Physical comedy.
Hebrew adjective used as noun with article.
Hebrew comparative כְּ + Algonquian אֲסוּן (stone) + animate plural -אַק. Stones are animate—they participate in the world.
Lenape asun. Takes animate plural because stones matter, they're participants in the world.
Hebrew karsulayim, dual form. Body vocabulary.
Hebrew wayyiqtol passive for lights coming on.
Hebrew passive participle. State of holding.
Hebrew participle. State of being down.
Hebrew wayyiqtol plural. Shared laughter without specified subject.
Hebrew weqatal construction. Converts one-time story into permanent pattern.
Hebrew weqatal for consequential future action.
Algonquian stem for 'cups' + Hebrew possessive suffix -הֶם. Hybrid morphology.
Lenape lənuw. Base form before plural.
Algonquian person prefix. Attaches to verbs and possessed nouns.
Algonquian suffix marking place: in, at, on, beside.
Algonquian suffix for smallness, endearment, young age.
Algonquian suffix marking 'the other one' in discourse tracking.
Algonquian suffix for plural of animate nouns.
Hebrew conjunction. The thread stitching clauses together.
Hebrew definite article. Attaches happily to Algonquian nouns.
Hybrid name: Mahican Mahicannituck ('river that flows both ways') + Hebrew territorial suffix -ítakh. The homeland.
Algonquian ininaatigo naaminas. Food vocabulary of the land.
Algonquian: full + shines + night-sun. Astronomical vocabulary.
Ojibwe boozhoo. Greeting from Central Algonquian.
Hebrew hayyom for abstract time; Lenape elemi for 'sometime today.'
